title: How EOF came out of Fusaka
intro: EOF, the EVM object format, was a plan to let Ethereum improve the EVM without breaking the contracts already live, by adding a new, validated kind of contract. Its champions saw faster code and simpler tools; others worried about complexity, risk and whether builders could use it. This map follows the debate from the first forum post in 2021 to the call that took EOF out of the Fusaka upgrade, and what came after, in talks from the client developers who argued it on the All Core Devs calls and in the research posts, forum replies and blogs that carried much of the argument.

stops.author: vbuterin
stops.source_title: EOF proposal: ban code introspection of EOF accounts
stops.note: The argument that made EOF bigger: if the EVM can be converted from one version to the next, it can keep improving without piling up old rules, but only if code cannot read itself. Handle shown as the forum shows it (vbuterin); no real name appears in the post, so no speaker link. Tim Beiko names Vitalik as the author of this thread on All Core Devs #152.

lines.text: One of the arguments against any EVM changes is that it's much harder to add features to the EVM than to remove them (eg. the complexities around even removing a little-used opcode like SELFDESTRUCT), and so if the EVM keeps changing, ever-increasing ugliness and complexity is likely to be the outcome.

One way to greatly reduce this tradeoff is to find a way to automatically convert version n EVM code to version n+1 EVM code every time there is an upgrade (not necessarily immediately; perhaps convert when old code is "touched", and make sure that all version n code is converted to version n+1 before attempting to implement version n+2).
Ban EOF-formatted code from being read with CODECOPY, CODESIZE, EXTCODECOPY, EXTCODESIZE and EXTCODEHASH

stops.author: Marius van der Wijden
stops.source_title: Why I am against EOF in Pectra
stops.note: The Geth side in writing, while EOF was planned for Pectra: complexity and consensus risk, no impact analysis, and a preference for Verkle. Tim Beiko's May 2025 post links to it as the strong opposition from core developers.

lines.text: The biggest issue I see is that EOF is extremely complex.
All-in-all EOF introduces 19 new opcodes. Additionally it removes 16 opcodes present in the existing EVM from EOF and changes the behavior of multiple opcodes in both versions.

Additionally EOF introduces the code and stack validation. This means that the code is verified before it’s being deployed. Therefore the code validity now becomes part of consensus which means that bugs in the code or stack validation will result in consensus bugs.

I personally believe that L1 should stop shipping small incremental improvements and should focus on big unlocks like 4844 and Verkle. These changes will really enable new things to be built on Ethereum, while EOF in my opinion only makes existing things slightly faster or slightly cheaper.

lines.text: The EVM Object Format is a long awaited upgrade that modernizes the EVM and removes obstacles that have wide-ranging effects on the entire language, tooling and application ecosystem on Ethereum. Solidity is in full support of the proposal and in this post we would like to explain why.

It is undeniable that the Ethereum clients bear most of the maintenance burden of this change as they will have to support both EOF and the legacy EVM for the foreseeable future. The benefits to clients of adopting EOF are also much less obvious.

If the argument is that there should be no changes on the execution layer at all, our opinion is that it is way too early to ossify it.

stops.title: Removed from Fusaka
stops.body: Core developers decided on this call to take EOF out of the Fusaka upgrade, and the notes record it as Declined for Inclusion. Tim Beiko's written reasons: the risk to Fusaka's timeline when shipping PeerDAS quickly came first, a variant whose implications some on the call realised they did not understand, and objections raised each time EOF was approved that the process never resolved. Several client teams had backed EOF, and its champions could make the case again for Glamsterdam.

The reasons are those copied into the notes from Tim Beiko's text in EIPs PR #9703 (EIP-7607 update). Notes list the call stream as youtube.com/watch?v=GcA-sVRSCHc; the recording link in the brief was M3DWaWbIB3s. Re-read on 6 Nov 2026: EIPs PR #9703 ("Update EIP-7607: Remove EOF from Fusaka", closed with the change merged on 28 Apr 2025) carries the three reasons quoted; EIP-7607 is now Final and does not list EOF; EIP-7692 is marked Stagnant.

stops.title: Not in the next upgrade
stops.body: The meta EIP for Glamsterdam, EIP-7773, which is still under review, does not list EOF among the EIPs scheduled for inclusion. Fusaka, now final in EIP-7607, does not include it either, and EIP-7692, the EOF meta, is marked Stagnant. The Glamsterdam list does include EIP-8024, a backward-compatible version of the SWAPN, DUPN and EXCHANGE stack instructions that EIP-7692 had counted among EOF's EIPs. We found no upgrade that lists EOF.
stops.note: Primary sources, read on 6 Nov 2026: EIP-7773 (status Review, last edited 22 Oct 2026), section EIPs Scheduled for Inclusion: no EOF EIP; EIP-8024 listed. EIP-7607 (Final since 4 Feb 2026) lists no EOF EIP. EIP-7692 header: Stagnant Meta; it lists EIP-663 (SWAPN, DUPN and EXCHANGE) among the EOFv1 EIPs. EIP-8024 abstract: SWAPN, DUPN and EXCHANGE lifting the stack-depth limit of 16; its rationale notes that the alternative needed bytecode versioning (EOF). Glamsterdam headliners ePBS and BALs are named in ralexstokes's post of 12 Nov 2025 (stop w-stokes-2025). The Besu Glamsterdam position paper (undated) says its EOF implementation is complete but defers it; not quoted.
